author: high4
claim: Every red-blue coloring of the edges on six vertices has a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Fix any vertex v. Its five incident edges have two colors, so at least three, say va, vb, vc, have the same color by the pigeonhole principle. If at least one of ab, bc, ca has that same color, it forms a monochromatic triangle with v. Otherwise all three edges ab, bc, ca have the other color, so abc is a monochromatic triangle. author: high4
claim: There is a red-blue coloring of the edges on five vertices with no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Label the vertices 0,1,2,3,4. Color red exactly the five edges 01,12,23,34,40, and color the remaining five edges blue. The red graph is the 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, hence contains no triangle. The blue graph is the 5-cycle 0-2-4-1-3-0, hence also contains no triangle. Thus no triangle is monochromatic. author: high2
claim: Every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Fix a vertex v. Among its five incident edges, at least three have one common color. Let their other endpoints be a,b,c. If one of ab,bc,ca has that common color, it and v form a monochromatic triangle. If none does, then ab,bc,ca all have the opposite color, so abc is a monochromatic triangle.

glossary.a, b, c: three distinct neighbors of v joined to v by edges of one common color

author: high2
claim: There is a red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Label the vertices 0,1,2,3,4 cyclically. Color the five cycle edges 01,12,23,34,40 red and all remaining edges blue. The red graph is the 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, so it has no triangle. The blue graph is the 5-cycle 0-2-4-1-3-0, so it also has no triangle.

author: high2
claim: The two bounds together are equivalent to R(3,3)=6.
evidence: By definition, R(3,3) is the least positive integer n such that every red-blue coloring of the complete graph on n vertices contains a monochromatic triangle. The six-vertex result gives R(3,3) at most 6, while the five-vertex construction gives R(3,3) greater than 5. Since R(3,3) is an integer, it equals 6.

author: high6
claim: In every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices, a fixed vertex has three incident edges of one color; the three corresponding neighbors either yield a triangle of that color with the fixed vertex or themselves form a triangle of the other color.
evidence: Fix a vertex v. Its five incident edges have two possible colors. If each color occurred on at most two of them, there would be at most four incident edges, so one color occurs on at least three edges va, vb, vc. If one of ab, ac, bc has that same color, it and the two corresponding edges through v form a monochromatic triangle. Otherwise all of ab, ac, bc have the other color, and abc is monochromatic.

author: high6
claim: There is a red-blue coloring of the complete graph on vertices 0,1,2,3,4 with no monochromatic triangle: color the edges of the cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0 red and all remaining edges blue.
evidence: The red graph is the 5-cycle in the stated order. For any vertex, its two red neighbors are not red-adjacent, so no red triangle exists. The blue edges form the 5-cycle 0-2-4-1-3-0. For any vertex, its two blue neighbors in this cycle are not blue-adjacent, so no blue triangle exists. Thus there is no monochromatic triangle.

author: high5
claim: In any red-blue coloring of the edges of K_6, choosing one vertex and three incident edges of a common color reduces the upper bound to the colors of the three edges among the other endpoints.
evidence: A chosen vertex has five incident edges, so one of the two colors appears on at least three of them: if each color appeared at most twice, there would be at most four incident edges. Let the three corresponding endpoints be a,b,c. If any of ab,bc,ca has the common incident color, it and the two incident edges through the chosen vertex give a monochromatic triangle. If none does, then all three are the other color and abc is a monochromatic triangle.

author: high7
claim: Prove that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle, while there is a red-blue coloring of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle. Equivalently, prove that the Ramsey number \(R(3,3)\) equals \(6\).
evidence: Upper bound: choose a vertex v in an arbitrary red-blue colored complete graph on six vertices. Among its five incident edges, at least three have one common color C, since otherwise each of the two colors appears at most twice and there would be at most four incident edges. Let a,b,c be the other endpoints of three such C-colored edges. If one of ab,ac,bc has color C, it and v form a C-colored triangle; otherwise all three of ab,ac,bc have the other color D and a,b,c form a D-colored triangle. Lower bound: on vertices 0,1,2,3,4 color 01,12,23,34,40 red and 02,24,41,13,30 blue. For each vertex its two red neighbors are joined by a blue edge: respectively 14,02,13,24,30. Thus there is no red triangle. Its two blue neighbors are joined by a red edge: respectively 23,34,40,01,12. Thus there is no blue triangle. Hence the coloring has no monochromatic triangle. Deleting vertices also gives such colorings on every smaller number of vertices. Therefore the Ramsey threshold is exactly six.
